entry.title: Nothing to lose is not nothing to spare.
entry.titleHtml: Nothing to lose is not nothing to spare.
entry.dek: Same coin, same flips: betting everything turns €100 into €34.87, betting a tenth turns it into €108.29. The risk is not the bet, it is what you cannot afford to lose.
body: “The same bet can be brave for one person and reckless for the next.”

Have you ever asked yourself why the same piece of advice can be right for one person and dangerous for another? Today is Friday, the 13th of November, the one day of the year when everybody pretends to care about luck, and yesterday I wrote about how luck gets edited out of every success story. Today I want to look at the other side of the same coin (and yes, there will be a coin). The advice I mean is one I have heard more times than I can count since I turned eighteen: “take risks while you are young, you have nothing to lose.” So the question is: is that true, and if it is, for whom? Let’s start from the beginning.

I met this idea properly in the same book as yesterday. In “The Psychology of Money”, “Luck & Risk” is not the only chapter I skipped in my review. There is another one, called “Room for Error”, and its point is simple: the most important thing is not how big the win can be, it is whether you can survive the loss. Housel has a line for it: “The most important part of every plan is planning on your plan not going according to plan.” When I put that next to the advice everybody gives students, I noticed that the advice only talks about one half of the story. It talks about the win. It never asks what you can afford to lose.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do, because “nothing to lose” and “nothing to spare” sound almost the same, and I think that is exactly why people mix them up. Nothing to lose means that if it goes wrong, you are back where you started, and where you started was fine - you live with your parents, nobody depends on you, the worst case is a bad year and a good story. Nothing to spare means that if it goes wrong, there is no “back where you started”, because the rent, the food or somebody else’s life was inside the bet. Two people can have exactly the same amount in their account and be on different sides of this line. <u>The advice is not about how much you have. It is about what happens to you if you lose it.</u>

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic, because this is where it surprised me. There is a coin game that the physicist Ole Peters uses to explain this, for example in his 2019 paper in Nature Physics, “The ergodicity problem in economics”. You start with €100. Every round you flip a coin. Heads, your money grows by 50%. Tails, it falls by 40%. On average, one round is worth:
0.5 × 1.5 + 0.5 × 0.6 = 1.05
So on average you win 5% per round, and if a thousand people each play one round, the group really does get richer. But you are not a thousand people. You are one person playing again and again, and over two rounds you will usually get one heads and one tails:
1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9
That is 10% lost every two rounds. After 20 rounds, with 10 heads and 10 tails: €100 × 0.910 = €34.87. A bet can be good on average and still ruin almost everybody who keeps playing it.

Now take the same game, but every round you only bet 10% of what you have. Heads, your total grows by 5%. Tails, it falls by 4%. Over two rounds:
1.05 × 0.96 = 1.008
After the same 20 rounds, 10 heads and 10 tails: €100 × 1.00810 = €108.29. Same coin, same odds, same luck (yes, you read that right, the exact same flips) - and one player ends with €34.87 while the other ends with €108.29. The only thing that changed is how much of everything was on the table. This is what I think “nothing to lose” really means: not that the bet is safe, but that the bet is small compared to what you have to protect.

Thirdly, I have to be fair to the advice, because it is not stupid. There is a reason losses are so dangerous, and it is simple maths. If you lose 10%, you need 11.1% to get back. If you lose 50%, you need 100%. If you lose 90%, you need 900%. The deeper the hole, the harder the climb, and that is exactly why the person with nothing to spare has to be careful. But the person with nothing to lose is in the opposite situation. At eighteen, the money I could lose is small, and the thing I have most of is time to recover. For me, being too careful also has a cost - it just never shows up on a bank statement. The job I did not apply for, the project I did not start, the blog I almost did not write. <u>Avoiding risk is also a risk, it is only a quieter one.</u>

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. Before the next risky thing I say yes to - money, time or anything else - I will write down two questions. The first: “If this goes completely wrong, what do I lose?” The second: “Can I still get up the next day and try again?” If the answer to the second one is yes, I will stop hiding behind being careful. If it is no, then it does not matter how good the average looks, I will make the bet smaller until the answer changes.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the line between nothing to lose and nothing to spare is the most useful thing I have learned about risk so far, but I have to be honest about two things. The coin game is clean in a way that life is not - real bets do not come with the odds written on them, and most of the time you do not even know if you are playing at 10% or at 100%. And “you have nothing to lose” is almost never fully true. Even at eighteen I can lose time, health or the trust of the people around me, and none of those come back at 1.5 per heads. What I take from it is smaller: before I ask how big the win could be, I ask how big the loss could be.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“The same bet can be brave for one person and reckless for the next.”
